content.text: Ruskin argues that noble ornament is disciplined abstraction: it expresses essential forms clearly, adapts design and workmanship to viewing distance, and remains subordinate to larger architectural masses. Medieval art best balances the governing designer with the freedom of lesser craftsmen, unlike servile Eastern imitation or Renaissance self-consciousness. Ornament should obey natural, structural, and hierarchical laws; avoid redundancy, excessive delicacy, rustication, and uncontrolled detail. He analyzes chamfers, dogtooth and dentils, bases, shafts, capitals, archivolts, roofs, and wall decoration, favoring robust simplicity, natural vitality, color, and truthful craftsmanship. Architecture should explain and preserve nature’s beauty rather than “correct” it, and good buildings should give urban life the joy and instruction of nature. He travels from Padua toward Venice, enters a gondola at Mestre, and rests in the upper room of the little inn there.
